cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain how the Scramble for Africa began and give examples in West Africa.

steps.text: Change in trade: from the 1800s the slave trade declined and Europeans turned to a new trade that needed permanent European settlement – the start of colonialism.
Britain: set up colonies in the Gold Coast and Sierra Leone.
France: created the largest colonial empire in West Africa, French West Africa (1900).

cards.title: North Africa -Egypt
body: Mohammed Ali established a separate empire in Egypt in 1805 known as the Mamluk dynasty .He modernized Egypt.
In 1854 the project of opening Suez Canal was started by French engineer Ferdinand de lespese and ended in 1869.
As the gate to three continents Suez Canal became strategically important and Britain bought share in 1875.
The Egyptians revolted in 1881 hating the European dominance, but it was crushed but Britain and Egypt became British protectorate in 1914.
Sudan became independent by the Mahdi revolution led by clerk Mohammed Ahmad in 1881 but British crush the revolution and Sudan became its colony.
Algeria starting from 1872 became French settler colony, soon France made morocco and Tunisia under her protectorate in 1912.
In north east Africa Italy set up colony in Eritrea and Somali but defeated in attempt to control Ethiopia in 1896.

cards.title: Model answer: North Africa under colonialism
cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe how European powers took control of North Africa.

steps.text: Egypt: Mohammed Ali modernised Egypt from 1805; the Suez Canal (1854–1869) became strategically vital and Britain bought shares in 1875; the 1881 revolt was crushed and Egypt became a British protectorate in 1914.
Sudan: the Mahdist revolution of 1881 was crushed by Britain, which made Sudan a colony.
French North Africa: Algeria became a French settler colony; Morocco and Tunisia became French protectorates in 1912.
North-east Africa: Italy took Eritrea and Somalia but was defeated in Ethiopia in 1896.

cards.answer: Britain took Egypt and Sudan, France took Algeria, Tunisia and Morocco, and Italy took Eritrea and Somalia – driven by the strategic Suez Canal and imperial rivalry.

cards.title: Central Africa
body: Central Africa became famous after the coming of the famous explorer David Livingstone in 1800s.

After his death henry Stanly continued his legacy and asked British for help but British refused. King Leopold 2ND of Belgium accepted him and he crated the largest colonial empire in central Africa .soon France also established colony here.

cards.title: Central Africa: from Livingstone to the Congo Free State
body: **Livingstone.** Arrived in **1841** and explored the interior for 30 years until his death in **1873**.

**Stanley.** Sent to find Livingstone, he stayed, explored the **Congo River** in the 1870s and sailed it to the Atlantic. Britain refused his settlement plan, so he turned to **King Leopold II** of Belgium, who hired him in **1876**.
**Scramble.** Leopold's claim to the Congo alarmed others; France quickly took the lands further north.
**Berlin decision.** The area along the Congo became the **Congo Free State**, run by Leopold with free trade and navigation – one of the harshest colonial regimes in Africa.
**Memory trick:** "Livingstone explored, Stanley sold, Leopold took."

cards.title: East Africa
body: In east Africa British and Germany rivaled for colonies .and agreed by the berlin conference .British took Kenya and Germany Tanzania and Zanzibar, Mozambique to Portugal and Rwanda to Belgium.

The Berlin Conference was conducted between 1884-85 in Germany to stop any conflicts between Europeans in Africa. The were asked just to register their colony between Berlin office to get recognition.

cards.title: East Africa and the Berlin Conference explained
body: **The rivals.** By 1885 Britain and Germany were the main rivals. Bismarck first saw colonies as unimportant but changed his mind as Germans demanded an empire. Britain wanted East Africa to link its territories from South Africa to Egypt.

**The Berlin Conference (1884–85).** Called by Bismarck: it recognized British and German claims in East Africa, gave Portugal **Mozambique**, created the **Congo Free State** under Leopold II, and in **Article 34** allowed powers to take African land if they notified the others.
**Why it matters.** Africans were not invited; the conference sped up the Scramble.
**Memory trick:** "Berlin: notify and take (Article 34)."

cards.title: Past exam (Model exam 2016)
cards.q: **Berlin conference** was held in 1884/85 to:

options.A: specify the conditions for African colonialism

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The **Berlin Conference** (1884–1885) was organized to regulate European colonization and trade in Africa. It established the principle of 'effective occupation,' which specified the conditions European powers had to meet to claim African territories.

**Step 2:** So the answer is A) specify the conditions for African colonialism.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.why:

**Step 2:** So the answer is D) Otto van Bismark.

cards.q: One of the following states was **not** British former colony:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “In east Africa British and Germany rivaled for colonies: Britain took Kenya, Germany took Tanzania, Mozambique went to Portugal and Rwanda to Belgium.”

**Step 2:** **Historical Fact:** 
- Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda were British colonies.
- **Rwanda** was originally a German colony (part of German East Africa) and later became a Belgian trust territory after WWI. It was never a British colony.

**Step 3:** So the answer is C) Rwanda.

cards.title: Completing this point: from the Great Trek to the Union of South Africa
body: **The Boers move north.** In the 1830s the Boers, descendants of 17th-century Dutch settlers, left the British Cape Colony and moved to the land between the Orange and Vaal rivers and north of the Vaal (the Great Trek).
**Two Boer republics.** There they founded the **Orange Free State** and the **Transvaal** (South African Republic).
**Conflict with the Zulu.** The Zulu kingdom built by **Shaka** stayed powerful after his death but was defeated by the British in the late 1800s.

**Rhodes and the Boer War.** Cecil Rhodes, owner of diamond and gold companies, pushed British expansion and took Rhodesia. After the war with the Boers, Britain created the **Union of South Africa (1910)**, a self-governing state where only whites, plus a few wealthy Africans, could vote.
**Memory trick:** "Trek (1830s) – Republics – Rhodes – Union (1910)."

cards.title: Comparing colonial rule in Africa
body: **By 1914** seven powers (Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal) had divided Africa; only **Liberia and Ethiopia** stayed independent.
**British indirect rule.** Local rulers enforced decisions made by British administrators; it was cheap but it hardened tribal divisions that caused conflict after independence.
**French and Italian direct rule.** A **governor-general** appointed from Europe ruled through a central bureaucracy.
**French assimilation.** Africans were expected to adopt French culture; a few could stand for office or sit in the French National Assembly.
**Nationalist reaction.** Western-educated Africans saw that colonizers preached democracy and equality but did not practise them in the colonies.
**Memory trick:** "Britain uses chiefs; France makes Frenchmen."

cards.title: Introdution
body: World War I (WW I), also known as the Great War, lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918.WW I was fought between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. The main members of the Allied Powers were France, Russia, and Britain. The United States also fought on the side of the Allies after 1917.The main members of the Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria.

cards.title: The causes of WWI: long-term and immediate
body: **Long-term causes (remember "MAN").** **M**ilitarism – the great powers built huge armies and navies; **A**lliances – the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, 1882) against the Triple Entente (France, Britain, Russia, 1907); **N**ationalism – each state put its national interest first and competed for colonies and trade.
**The Balkan spark.** Serbia, backed by Russia, wanted a large Slav state; Austria-Hungary annexed **Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908**, which angered Serbs.

**Immediate cause.** On **28 June 1914** Gavrilo Princip, a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb linked to the Black Hand, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife in **Sarajevo**. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war; the alliances pulled the other powers in within weeks.
**Exam tip:** Always separate the long-term causes (MAN) from the immediate cause (Sarajevo).

steps.text: Dates: 28 July 1914 – 11 November 1918 (the "Great War").

cards.title: Causes of the War
body: There was no single event that led to World War I. The war happened because of several different events that took place in the years building up to 1914.

The new international expansionist policy of Germany: In 1890 the new emperor of Germany, Wilhelm II, began an international policy that sought to turn his country into a world power. Germany was seen as a threat by the other powers and destabilized the international situation.

Mutual Defense Alliances: Countries throughout Europe made mutual defense agreements. These treaties meant that if one country was attacked, allied countries were bound to defend them. The Triple Alliance-1882 linking Germany with Austria-Hungary and Italy. The Triple Entente, which was made up of Britain, France, and Russia, concluded by 1907.Thus, there were two rival groups in Europe.

Imperialism: Before World War I, Africa and parts of Asia were points of contention among the European countries because of their raw materials. The increasing competition and desire for greater empires led to an increase in the confrontation that helped push the world into World War I.

Militarism: As the world entered the 20th century, an arms race had begun. By 1914, Germany had the greatest increase in military buildup. Great Britain and Germany both greatly increased their navies in this time period. This increase in militarism helped push the countries involved into war.

Nationalism: Much of the origin of the war was based on the desire of the Slavic peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina to no longer be part of Austria Hungary but instead be part of Serbia. In this way, nationalism led to the War.

cards.title: Model answer: long-term causes of the First World War
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the long-term causes of the First World War.

steps.text: Alliances: the Triple Alliance (1882: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) vs the Triple Entente (by 1907: Britain, France, Russia) – an attack on one drew in its allies.
Imperialism: competition for colonies and raw materials in Africa and Asia.
Militarism: an arms race – Germany's huge build-up and the naval race with Britain.
Nationalism: Slavs in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to join Serbia rather than stay in Austria-Hungary; Germany's world-power policy under Wilhelm II added tension.

cards.answer: Rival alliances, imperial competition, militarism and nationalism (remember MAIN) made a general war likely.

cards.title: The immediate cause
body: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand: In June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot while he was visiting Sarajevo in Bosnia. He was killed by a Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Principe , who thought that Serbia should control Bosnia instead of Austria. Because its leader had been shot, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. As a result Russia got involved as it had an alliance with Serbia. Germany then declared war on Russia because Germany had an alliance with Austria-Hungary.

Britain declared war on Germany because of its invasion of neutral Belgium - Britain had agreements to protect both Belgium and France. Some of the major battles during the war included the First Battle of the Marne, Battle of the Somme, Battle of Dannenberg, Battle of Gallipoli, and the Battle of Verdun.

lessons.title: Course of the First World War

cards.title: Course of the First World War
body: The conflict developed on several fronts in Europe, Africa, and Asia. The two main scenarios were the Western front, where the Germans confronted Britain, France and, after 1917, the Americans. The second front was the Eastern front in which the Russians fought against Germans and Austro-Hungarians.

cards.title: How the war was fought on the two fronts
body: **Western Front.** Germany planned to reach Paris quickly through **Belgium** (war on Belgium 4 August 1914) and got within 40 km of Paris, but was stopped at the **Marne** – France even rushed troops to the front in 2,000 Paris taxis.

**Stalemate.** Both sides dug trenches from the English Channel to Switzerland, protected by barbed wire, mines and machine guns, with "no-man's land" between them. Generals sent masses of men across after artillery barrages, and millions died; at **Verdun (1916)** about 700,000 died for a few kilometres.

**Eastern Front.** More mobile: Russia was beaten in eastern Germany, but Russia and Serbia drove Austria-Hungary out of Serbia; German help then defeated Russia (2.5 million casualties) and knocked Serbia out.
**New weapons.** Aircraft (first scouting, then attacking), submarines, machine guns, tanks and poison gas.
**Memory trick:** "West = trenches and stalemate; East = movement and huge losses."

cards.title: The western front
body: The war zone that included Belgium and northern France was called the Western Front. Germany had a plan to invade France through Belgium that’s why it invaded Belgium in august 4 which led to the entry of Great Britain to the war.

Once the Germans failed to reach Paris, the war quickly turned into a stalemate. Both the French and German forces dug hundreds of kilometers of trenches that stretched from the English Channel to the frontiers of Switzerland. These trenches were protected by barbed wire, land mines, and machine guns. They were separated from each other by a strip of territory known as no-man’s land.

The new method of fighting (Trench Warfare or War of Attrition) was new to the 1st world war generals. The no man’s land was unbreakable though they send thousands of soldiers. In 1916, for example, seven hundred thousand soldiers died over a few kilometers of land at Verdun, France.

cards.problem: (Exam question) Why did the Western Front become a stalemate?

steps.text: Plan failed: Germany invaded France through Belgium but failed to reach Paris.
Trenches: both sides dug hundreds of kilometres of trenches from the English Channel to Switzerland, protected by barbed wire, mines and machine guns.
No-man's land: attacks across it cost thousands of lives for little ground.
Example: about 700,000 died at Verdun (1916) over a few kilometres – a war of attrition.

cards.answer: When the German advance stopped short of Paris, both sides dug in; defensive weapons made attacks across no-man's land suicidal, producing a war of attrition.

cards.title: II.The Eastern Front
body: On the Eastern Front, Russia and Serbia fought against Austria-Hungary, Germany, and Turkey. In contrast to the Western Front, the war on the Eastern Front was marked by mobility. The cost in lives, however, was equally enormous.

At the beginning of the First World War, the Russian army moved into eastern Germany. But, it was decisively defeated. On the other hand, Russia and Serbia defeated Austria-Hungary and threw it out of Serbia. To make matters worse, the Italians betrayed their German and Austrian allies and attacked Austria in May 1915.

After it was defeated by Russia and Serbia, Austria-Hungary got help from its ally, Germany. Then the combined forces of Germany and Austria-Hungary defeated the Russian army. Russia suffered a very heavy casualties of 2.5 million killed, captured or wounded. It was almost knocked out of the war. Encouraged by their success, Germany and Austria-Hungary attacked and eliminated Serbia from the war.

cards.title: Widening (Spread) of the War
body: After the stalemate in western front different empires and countries were drawn to the war. Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria joined the central powers in 1915 .On May 1915 Italy turned to the allies. By 1917, the war that started in Europe became a world war. Britain encouraged Ottoman provinces in the Middle East to revolt against the Ottoman Empire. In 1918, British forces destroyed the Ottoman Empire in the Middle East. The Allied powers also took advantage of Germany’s preoccupation in Europe and its lack of naval power to seize German colonies in Africa and elsewhere. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and China also joined the war on the side of the Allies.

cards.title: Why the USA entered the war (1917)
body: **Blockades.** Britain blockaded Germany; Germany answered with unrestricted submarine warfare. **Lusitania (May 1915).** About 1,100 civilians, over 100 of them Americans, were killed; Germany paused its attacks. **1917.** Germany restarted unrestricted submarine warfare; the USA declared war in **April 1917**, and by 1918 over a million American soldiers were in Europe, tipping the balance.
**Memory trick:** "Subs sank ships, so the States stepped in."

cards.title: The entry of USA
body: At first the United States tried to remain neutral. As World War I continued, however, it became more and more difficult to remain neutral. The immediate cause of the United States entry into the war was a naval conflict between Germany and Great Britain.

In May 1915, a British ship named Lusitania was sunk by a German submarine. As a result, about 1100 civilians, including over 100 Americans, were killed. This greatly angered the United States. After strong opposition from the US, Germany stopped its unrestricted submarine attacks in 1915.

However Germany restarted sinking hundreds of allied ships killing thousands of civilians and On May 1917 USA officially entered in to the war sending one million troops. This greatly shifted the balance of power to the favor of the allies.

cards.title: 7.3 The Russian Revolution
body: The Russian revolution was a clash between the aristocratic monarchy of Tsar Nicholas 2nd and the people of Russia. The people specifically demanded peace and bread (the withdrawal of Russia from WW1 and economic reforms. Several causes led to the revolution of 1917 such as:
Industrially and technologically weak army.
Economic disasters caused by the war.
Tsar Nicholas 2 frequently usage of the army to suppress the people.

cards.title: Completing this point: causes and course of the Russian Revolution of 1917
body: **Causes.** (1) Russia was not ready for war – poor leaders and weak industry; two million soldiers died in 1914–1916 and four to six million were wounded or captured. (2) The war wrecked the economy. (3) Tsar Nicholas II ruled by force.

**February/March revolution.** Bread rationing in Petrograd led to protests; on **8 March 1917** (International Women's Day) about 10,000 women marched shouting "Peace and Bread". Soldiers refused to fire and joined them. The Duma set up a provisional government, and the tsar abdicated on 15 March.

**Bolsheviks take over.** Kerensky's provisional government stayed in the war. Lenin returned in April promising "Peace, Land, Bread" and "All Power to the Soviets", and on the night of **6 November 1917** the Bolsheviks seized the Winter Palace.
**Memory trick:** "War + Want + Whip = Revolution."

**Step 1:** From the lesson: “The Russian revolution was a clash between the aristocratic monarchy of Tsar Nicholas 2nd and the people of Russia.”

**Step 2:** **Analysis:** 
- **Causes (A, B, C, E):** Economic hardship, food shortages (bread riots), heavy military losses in WWI, and the absolute, suppressive rule of the Czar were all primary causes of the revolution.
- **The Assassination (D):** Czar Nicholas II and his family were assassinated in July 1918, which was a **consequence** or an event during the civil war *after* the revolution had already started in 1917.

**Step 3:** So the answer is D) Assassination of Czar Nicholas II.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.title: The Beginning of the Revolution
body: In February 1917, the Russian government started bread rationing in the then capital city of Russia Petrograd (formerly known as St. Petersburg) after the price of bread had risen sharply. However this erupted an uprising in the capital city by thousands of women on 10th March, 1917. As usually Tsar Nicholas 2nd ordered the troops to fire upon the mob but the soldiers refused and sided with the uprising. This eventually ignited the 1917 revolution.

cards.title: From bread riots to the tsar's abdication (March 1917)
body: **Step 1 – hunger.** Bread prices rose sharply and rationing began in Petrograd in February 1917.
**Step 2 – the women march.** On **8 March** (International Women's Day) about 10,000 women marched shouting "Peace and Bread" and "Down with the Czar"; other workers joined and factories closed.
**Step 3 – the army changes sides.** Soldiers ordered to fire refused and joined the protesters.
**Step 4 – new government.** On **12 March** the Duma set up a **provisional government**; Nicholas II abdicated on **15 March 1917**.
**Step 5 – dual power.** Kerensky's provisional government stayed in the war, while the **soviets** (workers' and soldiers' councils, strongest in Petrograd) opposed it – which gave Lenin his chance.
**Memory trick:** "Bread → Women → Soldiers → Duma → Abdication."

cards.title: The effects of the revolution
body: On 12 March 1917, the Russian legislative body known as Duma established a provisional government headed by Alexander Kerensky.
The provisional government decided to continue Russia’s involvement in the First World War.
The above decision led to protest from different protest groups especially the Soviets (The Soviets were local councils composed of representatives of Russian workers and soldiers).

The rise of the Bolsheviks; ‘Bolsheviks’ meaning majority in Russian, was a small faction of the Russian Marxist party known as the Social Democratic party. It was formed by a Russian Marxist named Vladimir I. Lenin in 1903.

Lenin and his comrades arrived at Petrograd, they began to unite the Soviets. They promised the people the following three things: “Peace, Land, Bread;” “Worker Control of Production;” “All Power to the Soviets.”
In November 6, 1917, the Bolshevik forces seized the Winter Palace (the seat of the provisional government). The provisional government quickly collapsed with little bloodshed.

steps.text: Provisional government: set up by the Duma under Kerensky (March 1917), but it continued the unpopular war.
Opposition: the Soviets of workers and soldiers protested.
Bolsheviks: Lenin's faction of the Social Democrats united the Soviets with the slogans "Peace, Land, Bread", "Worker control of production" and "All power to the Soviets".
Seizure of power: on 6 November 1917 the Bolsheviks seized the Winter Palace and the provisional government collapsed with little bloodshed.

lessons.title: The result of the October 1917 revolution war

cards.title: The result of the October 1917 revolution war
body: The congress appointed Lenin as head of the new government (communist).
In March 1918, Lenin signed the peace treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany and ended Russia’s involvement in the war.
Besides, the Bolshevik government nationalized all land and distributed them to the peasants.
The rise of civil war because of the opposition groups like the royalists, anti-Lenin socialists, and liberals.
The liberals in general known as the white force helped by the allied forces fought against the red army of the Bolsheviks .The red army decisively won in 1920.

cards.title: The Russian Civil War (1918–1921)
body: **Two sides.** The **Reds** (Communists) against the **Whites** – liberals, anti-Lenin socialists and royalists, backed by the Allies (at one point over 100,000 Allied troops were in Russia).
**Outcome.** The Red Army defeated most Whites by 1920 and controlled all Russia in 1921.
**The royal family.** Held in the Urals, the tsar, his wife and five children were killed by the local Soviet on the night of **16 July 1918**.
**Memory trick:** "Red beat White, 1918–21."

lessons.title: The end of the first World War

cards.title: The end of the first World War
body: Finally after the German offensive in the spring of 1918, the Allied counterattack managed to force a decisive retreat of the German army. The defeat of its Germany’s allies and the revolution in Germany that dethroned Wilhelm II (German Emperor), brought about the signing of the armistice on November 11, 1918. The Great War was over.

cards.title: How WWI ended, step by step
body: **1917 – mixed year.** Allied attacks on the Western Front failed and Russia left the war after the November revolution, but US entry raised Allied morale.
**March 1918 – Germany's last gamble.** Free from the Eastern Front, Germany attacked in the west and by April was within about 80 km of Paris.
**The turn.** French, Moroccan and American troops with hundreds of tanks stopped the advance; with over a million Americans in France the Allies counter-attacked and pushed steadily towards Germany.

**Collapse at home.** Defeats and hardship led to a German army mutiny in November 1918; workers' and soldiers' councils took over in the north, and **Emperor William II** left the country on **9 November**.
**Armistice.** The new government signed it on **11 November 1918**; Germany's allies (Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Bulgaria) had already given up.
**Cost.** Over 10 million soldiers and at least 1 million civilians died, and 20 million were wounded.
**Memory trick:** "11th hour, 11th day, 11th month, 1918."

cards.title: Consequences of the war
body: Economic consequences: World War I cost the participating countries a lot of money. Germany and Great Britain spent about 60% of the money their economy produced. Countries had to raise taxes and borrow money from their citizens. They also printed money in order to buy weapons and other things they needed for war. This led to inflation after the war.

Political Consequences: World War I brought an end to four monarchies: Czar Nicholas II of Russia, Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany, Emperor Charles of Austria and the sultan of the Ottoman Empire had to step down.

New countries were created out of old empires: Austria- Hungary was carved up into a number of independent states. Russia and Germany gave land to Poland. Countries in the Middle East were put under the control of Great Britain and France. What was left of Ottoman Empire became Turkey.

Social Consequences: World war changed society completely. Birth rates declined because millions of young men died (eight million died, millions wounded, maimed (to lose limbs), widows and orphans). Civilians lost their land and fled to other countries.
The role of women also changed. They played a major part in replacing men in factories and offices. Many countries gave women more rights after the war had ended, including the right to vote.
The upper classes lost their leading role in society. Young middle and lower class men and women demanded a say in forming their country after the war.

cards.title: Treaty of Versailles: On June 28, 1919
body: World War I officially ended with the signing of the Treaty of Versailles. The Treaty of Versailles was an attempt to prevent the world from going into another war. It is organized in several chapters each having different clauses.

cards.title: The Paris Peace Conference and the main terms of Versailles
body: **The Big Four.** Wilson (USA), Clemenceau (France), Lloyd George (Britain) and Orlando (Italy). Wilson wanted a League of Nations and borders based on nationality; France wanted huge reparations and a buffer state on the Rhine; Britain wanted reparations. The result was a compromise.
**Five treaties.** With Germany, Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and Turkey; Versailles (with Germany) was the most important.

**Four key terms.** (1) **War guilt** – Germany was responsible and must pay **reparations**; (2) army cut to **100,000** men, navy reduced, no air force; (3) **Alsace-Lorraine** returned to France; (4) the **Rhineland** demilitarized.
**Why it mattered.** Germans saw it as a harsh, humiliating dictated peace – one root of WWII.
**Memory trick:** "Guilt, Guns, Ground, Gold" – blame, disarmament, lost land, reparations.

cards.title: Model answer: the Treaty of Versailles
cards.problem: (Exam question) What were the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles (1919)?

steps.text: Date and aim: signed on 28 June 1919 to end WWI and prevent another war.
Territory: France regained Alsace-Lorraine, Poland took eastern lands, Danzig became a free city, and Germany lost all its colonies.
Military: the German army was limited to 100,000 troops, with no tanks, aircraft or heavy artillery, a much smaller navy and a demilitarised Rhineland.
Reparations: Germany and its allies were declared responsible for all loss and damage and had to pay.

cards.answer: Germany lost territory and all colonies, was disarmed (100,000-man army, demilitarised Rhineland) and had to pay reparations as the guilty party.

cards.title: Territorial clauses
body: *France regained Alsace and Lorraine from Germany.
*Eupen and Malmedy passed into the hands of Belgium from Germany.
*Eastern territories were annexed by Poland which caused East Prussia to become territorially isolated.
*Danzig and Memel, former Baltic German cities were declared free cities.
*Denmark annexed northern Schleswig-Holstein.
*Germany lost all of its colonies and the victors annexed them.
Military clauses:
*Drastic limitation of the German navy. Dramatic reduction of the Army (only 100,000 troops, prohibition of having tanks, aircraft and heavy artillery).
*Demilitarization of the Rhineland region.

cards.title: The wider territorial changes after WWI
body: **Empires broken up.** Austria-Hungary disappeared; Germany and Russia lost land in Eastern Europe. **New states.** Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Austria and Hungary. **Ottoman lands.** Despite promises to the Arabs, France took **Syria and Lebanon** and Britain took **Iraq and Palestine** as League of Nations **mandates**.
**Memory trick:** "Four empires fell, eight states rose."

cards.title: War Reparations
body: The treaty declared Germany and its allies responsible for all 'loss and damage' suffered by the Allies and as a consequence they were forced to pay war reparations to the victors.

cards.title: Reparations: the numbers and the consequences
body: **The bill.** In April 1921 the Allied Reparations Commission set the total at **132 billion gold marks** (about 33 billion US dollars), paid in yearly instalments. Germany made its first payment in 1921.

**The crisis.** In 1922 Germany said it could not pay. In 1923 France occupied the **Ruhr**, Germany's industrial heart, to take payment in coal and goods. German workers went on strike and the government paid them by printing money.
**Hyperinflation.** In 1914 one dollar bought 4.2 marks; by November 1923 one dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks, and savings were wiped out.
**The fixes.** The **Dawes Plan (1924)** lowered yearly payments according to Germany's ability to pay and gave a $200 million US loan, bringing a short prosperity (1924–29).
**The long-term effect.** Reparations caused resentment that Hitler used against the "Versailles dictate".
**Memory trick:** "132 billion → Ruhr → Runaway prices → Rescue (Dawes)."

cards.title: Other Treaties
body: *The Treaty of Neuilly, signed with Bulgaria. The small Balkan country suffered several territorial losses, in the benefit of Romania, Greece and a brand-new country: Yugoslavia.

*The Treaty of Sevres (1920) signed with Turkey .The Treaty of Sevres was extremely hard and led to the Turkish national rebellion, which was led by Kemal Ataturk. This also led to the war against Greece, which occupied large areas of Anatolia.
*other important social and ideological changes The U.S., which had won the war but had not experienced the conflict on its territory, became a first world power.
The triumph of the Soviet Revolution (Russian Revolution) and the social crisis that followed the war encouraged workers in many countries to protest, creating a pre-revolutionary climate.

The extreme nationalism experienced during the war, coupled with fear of a Communist revolution, encouraged the middle-class populations of some countries to move to the extreme right. This created a hotbed of fascist movements.

Creation of the League of Nations: The League of Nations was an international diplomatic group developed after World War I as a way to solve disputes between countries before they erupted into open warfare. A precursor to the United Nations, the League achieved some victories but had a mixed record of success.

tips.text: World War I (WW I), also known as the Great War, lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918.WW I was fought between the Allied Powers and the Central Powers. The main members of the Allied Powers were France, Russia, and Britain. The United States also fought on the side of the Allies after 1917.The main members of the Central Powers were Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria.
There was no single event that led to World War I. The war happened because of several different events that took place in the years building up to 1914.

Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand: In June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot while he was visiting Sarajevo in Bosnia. He was killed by a Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Principe , who thought that Serbia should control Bosnia instead of Austria. Because its leader had been shot, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. As a result Russia got involved as it had an alliance with Serbia. Germany then declared war on Russia because Germany had an alliance with Austria-Hungary.

The conflict developed on several fronts in Europe, Africa, and Asia. The two main scenarios were the Western front, where the Germans confronted Britain, France and, after 1917, the Americans. The second front was the Eastern front in which the Russians fought against Germans and Austro-Hungarians.

The war zone that included Belgium and northern France was called the Western Front. Germany had a plan to invade France through Belgium that’s why it invaded Belgium in august 4 which led to the entry of Great Britain to the war.

On the Eastern Front, Russia and Serbia fought against Austria-Hungary, Germany, and Turkey. In contrast to the Western Front, the war on the Eastern Front was marked by mobility. The cost in lives, however, was equally enormous.

After the stalemate in western front different empires and countries were drawn to the war. Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria joined the central powers in 1915 .On May 1915 Italy turned to the allies. By 1917, the war that started in Europe became a world war. Britain encouraged Ottoman provinces in the Middle East to revolt against the Ottoman Empire. In 1918, British forces destroyed the Ottoman Empire in the Middle East. The Allied powers also took advantage of Germany’s preoccupation in Europe and its lack of naval power to seize German colonies in Africa and elsewhere. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and China also joined the war on the side of the Allies.

At first the United States tried to remain neutral. As World War I continued, however, it became more and more difficult to remain neutral. The immediate cause of the United States entry into the war was a naval conflict between Germany and Great Britain.

lessons.title: Europe and USA in the Interwar Period

cards.title: Focus question: What does it mean by interwar period?
body: The term “interwar” refers to the period that stretches from the end of the First World War in 1919 to the beginning of the Second World War in 1939.
The interwar period was characterized by difficult economic problems and emergence of dictatorial regimes in Italy, Germany, Russia, and Eastern Europe.
Elsewhere in Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Latin America (South America), the interwar period was characterized by the rise of nationalism and national movements.

cards.title: The Great Depression: the key event of the interwar years
body: **What it was.** The collapse of Western economies at the end of the 1920s and in the 1930s – low economic activity and mass unemployment.

**Causes.** Fundamental: uneven distribution of wealth and an unregulated free market. Immediate: economic decline in many Western countries in the late 1920s, and the financial crisis when US investors pulled money out of Germany for the booming stock market, which then **crashed in October 1929**.

**Effects.** In 1932 one British worker in four and about 6 million Germans (40 %) were unemployed; Americans suffered hunger and homelessness. Despair strengthened extreme parties, which paved the way for dictatorships and WWII.
**Memory trick:** "Crash 1929, Jobless 1932, Dictators 1933."

cards.title: Efforts for Peace and Security
body: The peace settlement at the end of World War I had sought to bring peace among the warring states. It created the League of Nations to guarantee collective peace and security.

From the beginning, however, the peace settlement left many states unhappy. Eastern Europe was beset by border disputes and many Germans felt bitter about the Treaty of Versailles and vowed to revise it.
Some of the weakness of the league of nations was:
The absence of powerful countries like USA, JAPAN, ITALY and LATER GERMANY also withdraw.
Lack of army made the league unable to implement its decisions.
Some of the events that the league of nations failed to stop include:
Failed to stop border dispute in Eastern Europe.
Failed to stop japan invasion of china territory called Manchuria in 1931.
Failed Germany invasion of Poland and Czechoslovakia in 1939 and 1938 respectively.
Failed to stop Italian invasion of Ethiopia in 1936. And other more.

cards.title: Completing these points: why the League of Nations was weak
body: **Weakness 1 – missing great powers.** The US Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, so the USA never joined. Germany and Russia were outside for many years, and Japan, Germany and Italy later walked out.
**Weakness 2 – no army.** It had no power to enforce its decisions or stop aggression; it could only condemn or apply economic sanctions.

**Failures.** Japan's invasion of **Manchuria (1931)**; Italy's invasion of **Ethiopia (1935)** despite sanctions; Germany's rearmament, the Rhineland (1936), Austria and Czechoslovakia (1938) and Poland (1939).
**Memory trick:** "No USA, No Army, No Success."

cards.title: The Question of Reparation
body: Between 1919 and 1924, France demanded a strict enforcement of the Treaty of Versailles. It pressured Germany to pay the reparations agreed in the Treaty. In April 1921, the Allied Reparations Commission decided that Germany pay 132 billion German Marks (33 billion U.S. dollars), payable in annual installment of 2.5million Marks. Germany made its first payment in 1921.

By the following year, however, the German government announced that it was unable to pay any more because of financial problems. France was outraged and sent troops to occupy the Ruhr Valley, Germany’s main industrial and mining center. As a result, German workers went on strike, and their government paid them salaries by printing more paper money. Printing more paper money resulted in higher inflation in Germany.

The economic problems in Germany created unemployment, hyperinflation, loss of life time savings and etc. Strikes by German workers of the Ruhr and British and American protests against the occupation forced France to withdraw from the Ruhr Valley. In August 1924, an international commission produced a new plan for reparations. This new plan was known as the Dawes Plan, after the American banker who chaired the commission. The plan had two objectives:
Reduce the net payment Germany must pay annually based on its ability.
And give 200 million $ for recovery European and Germany economy.
A brief period of European prosperity followed, but it only lasted from 1924 to 1929.

cards.title: Completing this point: hyperinflation and the Dawes Plan
body: **Hyperinflation.** Germany paid striking Ruhr workers by printing money. In 1914, 1 US dollar = 4.2 marks; by November 1923, 1 dollar = 4.2 trillion marks. Savings were wiped out and workers carried their pay home in wheelbarrows.

**The Dawes Plan (August 1924).** Named after the American banker who chaired the commission: (1) it reduced reparations and linked yearly payments to Germany's ability to pay; (2) it gave a $200 million American loan, and US investment flowed into Europe.
**Result.** Prosperity from 1924 to 1929; Germany joined the League in 1926, and in 1928 sixty-three countries signed an accord rejecting war as national policy.
**Memory trick:** "Print → Price explosion → Plan (Dawes)."

cards.title: The Great Depression
body: A depression is a period of low economic activity and rising unemployment. It was start in 1920s and throughout 1930s,the economies of western countries collapsed. The great depression had big negative consequences on the social, economic, and political conditions of western countries It devastated public morale and led to the rise and strengthening of extreme political parties. The fundamental cause of the depression can be found in the inherent problems of capitalist economic system.
Uneven distribution of land and resource.
Unregulated free market.
The serious decline of economy.

The full United states stock market.1924s the U,S stock market gave to Germany loan under the Dawns plan. Germany needed the US loan to pay reparations to France and Great Britain. In October 1929, the US stock market crushed and the prices of stock collapsed.

In fear US investors withdrew even more money from Germany and other European markets. This withdrew even more money from Germany and other European market. As a result, industrial production declined, and unemployment rose.

cards.title: EFFECTS OF GERAT DEPRESSTION
body: Unemployment: During 1932,the worst year of depression, nearly one British worker in every four hours unemployed. About six million Germans or roughly 40% German labor force were out of work. Millions of Americans were left without adequate food, shelter, and clothing. However few people died from starvation.

Social changes: The economic crises had also affected the roles of men and women. Women able to get low paying jobs as servants, house cleaners and laundresses while many men remained unemployed, either begging on the streets rates or staying at home to do household tasks.

Political changes: the great depression also increased government activity in the economy. Another effect is the renewed interest in communism. Finally, the great depression led many people to join extreme parties such as the Nazis in Germany and the Fascist party in Italy.

cards.title: Past exam (Model exam 2024)

**Step 2:** Economic factors included the stock market crash, bank failures (financial crisis), overproduction, and wealth inequality.
**Step 3:** Socialism was a political ideology that gained popularity *because* of the Depression's failures in capitalist systems, but it did not cause the Depression.
**Result:** The spread of Socialism is not a cause.

**Step 2:** So the answer is D) The spread of Socialism.

cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the causes and effects of the Great Depression.

steps.text: Causes: problems of the capitalist system – uneven distribution of wealth, economic decline and the crash of the US stock market (October 1929).

lessons.title: Interwar Political Developments in Europe and U.S.A

cards.title: 1. EUROPE
body: In a number of European countries, women were allowed to vote. But countries such as France, Italy, and Switzerland did not allow women to vote. (Women gained the right to vote in1944 in France, in 1945 in Italy, and 1971 in Switzerland.)
In the 1920s, Europe seemed to be returning to normalcy. However, this was not an easy process.

cards.title: I.Germany
body: The Weimar Republic faced many problems from the beginning. One of the problems was the economy.
It pushed many of Germany’s middle class, like teachers and civil servants, toward political parties that were opposed to the Weimar Republic.
As a result of the Great Depression, about four and half million Germans became unemployed in 1930.
The depression created fear and insecurity among Germans and encouraged the rise of extremist parties like the Nazi.

cards.title: II. France
body: After the defeat of Germany in WWI, France became the strongest power in Europe.
However, France, too, suffered financial problems after the war.
France had a relatively stronger economy than other countries; it did not suffer the full impacts of the Great Depression until 1932.
The economic decline then led to political crises in the country. Between 1932 and 1933 only, six governments were formed as the country passed through political chaos.
Finally, in June 1936, a coalition of leftist parties formed a government known as the Popular Front government.
The Popular Front government gave French workers
The right to collective bargaining, i.e., the right of workers’ unions to negotiate with employers over wages and working hours.
In addition, the government fixed working hours to a 40-hour workweek in industry and granted two-week annual paid vacation to workers.

cards.title: III.Great Britain
body: Britain had lost many markets for its industrial products. In many places, the United States and Japan replaced Great Britain as the main exporters of industrial products.
British industries declined and the rate of unemployment increased. In 1921, two million Britons were unemployed.
Moreover, the return of large numbers of soldiers from the war pushed up prices and drove down wages.
As the British economy worsened, the conservative government broke apart. In 1924, the first labor government came to power promising to improve the conditions of British workers.
But, the labor government also failed to fulfill the needs of British workers. Therefore, after only one year in power, the labor government was brought down by a series of workers’ strikes in 1925.

The Labor party was elected in 1929 in coalition with the Liberal party. The coalition tried to introduce a program of social welfare and full employment. But before it started to implement its policies, the Great Depression began.
The depression hit Britain hard. Unemployment rose to 2.5 million within a year and to 3 million by the beginning of 1933. The Labor prime minister was forced to resign in 1931.

cards.title: The United States
body: Same as the powerful countries USA was faced unemployment, any suffered homelessness and starvation.
Under such terrible circumstances, a Democratic candidate named Franklin Delano Roosevelt won a landslide victory in the 1932 presidential election.
Roosevelt introduced a new policy of active government intervention in the economy known as the New Deal.
The policy of New Deal was aimed at creating recovery and reform. It also included relief for the homeless and destitute.

cards.problem: (Short answer) Describe interwar political developments in Germany, France and Britain.

steps.text: Germany: the Weimar Republic faced economic crisis; 4.5 million unemployed in 1930 pushed the middle class towards extremist parties like the Nazis.

France: the strongest power after 1918, but hit by depression from 1932; six governments fell in 1932–33 until the left-wing Popular Front (1936) gave workers collective bargaining, a 40-hour week and paid holidays.
Britain: lost markets to the USA and Japan; two million unemployed in 1921.
Women: many countries gave women the vote, but France (1944), Italy (1945) and Switzerland (1971) waited.

cards.title: Focus question
body: Have you ever heard of dictatorships? Explain what you understand by dictatorships?

In the 1930s, dictatorial or totalitarian regimes emerged in eastern and central Europe and elsewhere. A dictatorial or totalitarian government is a government that tries to control the political, economic, social, intellectual, and cultural lives of its citizens.

cards.title: Totalitarian governments have many characteristics in common. Some of them are
body: They want total obedience from their citizens and try to win popular support through massive propaganda.
They are led by a single leader and a political party.
They are opposed to individual freedoms and use security agencies to brutally suppress opponents.

cards.title: Completing this point: what "totalitarian" means
body: **Definition.** A totalitarian government tries to control the political, economic, social, intellectual and cultural lives of its citizens. In the 1920s most European states were democracies, but in the 1930s dictatorships spread in eastern and central Europe.
**The three common features.** (1) Total obedience, won through massive **propaganda**; (2) one **leader** and one **party**; (3) no individual freedom – **secret police** crush opponents.
**The best-known examples.** Fascist Italy (Mussolini), Nazi Germany (Hitler) and Stalin's Soviet Union.
**Memory trick:** "Propaganda, Party, Police" – the three P's of totalitarianism.

cards.title: Completing this point: Stalin's Soviet Union, the third dictatorship
body: **Rise.** After Lenin died in 1924, Stalin pushed out Trotsky and by 1929 had a complete dictatorship.

**Five-Year Plans (from 1928).** They aimed to turn Russia from an agricultural into an industrial country; heavy machinery, steel, coal and chemicals quadrupled, and literacy improved, so the USSR boomed while the West suffered the Great Depression.
**The cost.** Low wages and housing shortages left millions of workers poor, and private farms were abolished through **collectivization**.

**Compare.** Mussolini (Fascist party 1919) wanted to restore Roman glory; Hitler wanted to cancel Versailles and expand; Stalin wanted rapid industrial power – all three used one party, propaganda and terror.
**Memory trick:** "Stalin = Steel and Collective farms."

body: By the end of 1920s and the beginning of 1930s, most of these countries adopted dictatorial regimes. Czechoslovakia was an exception; it continued to be a democratic.

cards.title: Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal)
body: In Spain, the military led by General Francisco Franco revolted against the Republican government in 1936. As a result, the country entered into a brutal and bloody civil war between 1936 and 1939.The Spanish civil war was fought between two groups. The republicans and the military general Francisco Franco group.
The Spanish civil war ended when Franco’s forces defeated the Republicans in 1939.
Thereafter, Franco established a dictatorial government which lasted until 1975.

Similarly in Portugal, the Republican government was replaced by a military dictatorship in 1926. By the early 1930s, the Portuguese dictatorship was led by a man named Antonio Salazar. Salazar ruled Portugal for forty years.

lessons.title: Cultural Developments of the Interwar Period

cards.title: 1. Mass Culture: Radio and Movies
body: Some of the most important technological innovations that influenced the post First World War cultural developments were the:
Invention of radios and movie cameras.
Radio was invented by an Italian electrical engineer, Guglielmo Marconi, at the end of the 19th century.
On the other hand, movies (motion pictures) emerged in the 1890s. Shortly before WWI, full length movies began to emerge. After the end of WWI, cinema became a popular form of mass entertainment.

cards.title: Completing this point: radio and cinema in the interwar years
body: **Radio.** Invented by Marconi at the end of the 19th century, but first used for mass broadcasting in **1920**; stations were built in the USA, Europe and Japan in 1921–22, and radios became common in homes.

**Cinema.** Films appeared in the 1890s, feature-length films just before WWI, and after the war cinema became mass entertainment; by the late 1930s about 40 % of Western adults went to the cinema once a week.
**Politics.** Both were used as **propaganda** tools by governments, especially the dictatorships.
**Mass leisure.** The eight-hour day gave workers free time for sport, travel, concerts and films.
**Memory trick:** "Radio 1920, cinema weekly, propaganda always."

cards.title: 2. Mass Leisure in Europe
body: After WWI, the eight-hour workday became the normal practice for many office and factory workers in Europe.
This gave long free hours to many people. As a result, leisure activities; such as sporting events, travels, concerts, operas, and films, became common.
Travelling was made much easier by the production of trains, buses and cars. Thus, travelling became widespread pastime for many Europeans.

cards.title: 3. Artistic and Literary Developments
body: Most of the inter war period literary artistic works were based or meant to explain the misery created by the WW1 some of the works were:
In painting, two movements known as Dada and Surrealism emerged.
Dadaism was an artistic movement that was established by artists who believed that life has no purpose and meaning.
Surrealism was an artistic movement created by artists who tried to portray fantasies, dreams, and nightmares.
One of the most important post WWI writers was James Joyce. Joyce’s most famous book is the Ulysses.
Ulysses tells the story of one day in the life of ordinary people in Dublin by following the flow of their inner thoughts.

cards.title: Completing this point: why interwar art was so gloomy
body: **The mood.** WWI made many Europeans feel hopeless; people believed that humans were violent and incapable of building a rational world. The Great Depression and fascism deepened this despair.
**Painting.** **Dadaism** – life has no purpose or meaning; **Surrealism** – painting dreams, fantasies and nightmares (Salvador Dali's *Persistence of Memory*, with melting clocks).
**Literature.** Writers explored people's inner thoughts; James Joyce's *Ulysses* follows one day in Dublin through the flow of characters' thoughts.
**Memory trick:** "Dada = no meaning, Surreal = dreams, Joyce = inner thoughts."

cards.title: Model answer: interwar culture
cards.problem: (Short answer) Describe the cultural developments of the interwar period.

steps.text: Technology: radio (Marconi) and motion pictures; cinema became mass entertainment after WWI.
Leisure: the eight-hour day gave free time for sport, travel, concerts and films; trains, buses and cars made travel common.
Art: Dadaism (life has no purpose or meaning) and Surrealism (fantasies, dreams and nightmares).

cards.answer: Radio, cinema and more leisure created mass culture, while Dada, Surrealism and writers like James Joyce reflected the shock of the war.

cards.front: Focus question: What does it mean by interwar period?
cards.back: The term “interwar” refers to the period that stretches from the end of the First World War in 1919 to the beginning of the Second World War in 1939.
The peace settlement at the end of World War I had sought to bring peace among the warring states. It created the League of Nations to guarantee collective peace and security.

Between 1919 and 1924, France demanded a strict enforcement of the Treaty of Versailles. It pressured Germany to pay the reparations agreed in the Treaty. In April 1921, the Allied Reparations Commission decided that Germany pay 132 billion German Marks (33 billion U.S. dollars), payable in annual installment of 2.5million Marks. Germany made its first payment in 1921.

A depression is a period of low economic activity and rising unemployment. It was start in 1920s and throughout 1930s,the economies of western countries collapsed. The great depression had big negative consequences on the social, economic, and political conditions of western countries It devastated public morale and led to the rise and strengthening of extreme political parties. The fundamental cause of the depression can be found in the inherent problems of capitalist economic system.

Unemployment: During 1932,the worst year of depression, nearly one British worker in every four hours unemployed. About six million Germans or roughly 40% German labor force were out of work. Millions of Americans were left without adequate food, shelter, and clothing. However few people died from starvation.

In a number of European countries, women were allowed to vote. But countries such as France, Italy, and Switzerland did not allow women to vote. (Women gained the right to vote in1944 in France, in 1945 in Italy, and 1971 in Switzerland.)
The Weimar Republic faced many problems from the beginning. One of the problems was the economy.
After the defeat of Germany in WWI, France became the strongest power in Europe.

units.title: Nationalisms and National Movements around the World (1919-1939)

cards.title: Background
body: Between 1919 and 1939, national movements emerged in Africa and Asia. These movements sought to free their countries from European colonization.
Though none of the movements were not successful they left a legacy to the post ww2nd nationalist movement.

cards.title: Two kinds of nationalism between the wars
body: **Anti-colonial nationalism.** In Africa, the Middle East and Asia national movements aimed at **independence** from European colonial rule.

**Anti-domination nationalism.** In Latin America the countries were already independent but suffered Western, especially US, economic and political domination, so movements aimed to free their economies.

**Key events.** **1916** – the governor of Mecca, encouraged by Britain, declared Arabia independent of the Ottomans; **1923** – the Turkish Republic under Kemal Atatürk replaced the Ottoman Empire; **1928** – Chiang Kai-shek formed a new Chinese government; **1930** – Gandhi's **Salt March** in India against British law; **1931** – Japan invaded Manchuria; **1932** – Saudi Arabia was founded.
**Why they mostly failed then.** Colonial powers were still strong, but these movements trained leaders and ideas that won independence after WWII.
**Memory trick:** "Colonies wanted freedom; Latin America wanted economic freedom."

lessons.title: NATIONALISTS AND NATIONAL MOVMENTS IN AFRICA

cards.title: NATIONALISTS AND NATIONAL MOVMENTS IN AFRICA
body: Many Africans participated in the WW1st along side Britain and France hoping independence will be granted when the war ended but their hopes were betrayed.
Instead, former German colonies were awarded to Great Britain and colonial rule continued unchanged.
Africans became more active politically after the end of WWI. In many parts of Africa, movements emerged that demanded reform in the colonial system.
Although European colonial powers responded to such movements with force, they eventually began to make some reforms.

But the reforms introduced by the colonial powers did not satisfy many Africans Therefore, by the 1930s, a lot of Africans started to call for independence. These calls for independence came especially from a new generation of young African leaders. Most of these young leaders were educated abroad in Europe and the United States. Some of the most prominent new African leaders were Jomo Kenyatta of Kenya, Leopold Senghor of Senegal, Nnamdi Azikiwe of Nigeria.

The new African leaders were influenced by the ideas of Pan-Africanism. Pan-Africanism was an idea that proposed to unite all black Africans regardless of their national boundaries. Originally, it was popular in the United States and the Caribbean.

The two most prominent Pan- Africanists were W.E.B. Du Bois and Marcus Garvey. At the same time, an intellectual and cultural movement known as “Negritude” developed. Negritude sought to stress the uniqueness and importance of African culture and history.
Nationalism and National Movements in Asia A. Indian Movement for Independence
Mohandas Gandhi had become active in the Indian movement for self- rule before WWI. Because of his struggles, Indians had begun to call him India’s “Great Soul,” or Mahatma.
In protest, Gandhi organized numerous nonviolent protests and strikes against the British colonial system.

Gandhi was a believer in a nonviolent method of struggle. He protested British laws by using the methods of civil disobedience. Civil disobedience is a refusal to obey laws considered to be unjust and oppressive.

Gandhi based his ideas and methods of protest on the ancient Hindu idea of ahimsa, or reverence for life. He believed that the brutal British colonial rule could be defeated through love and non- violence. Gandhi called his non-violent acts of resistance, Satyagraha, a Sanskrit word for “truth and firmness.” The British response toward the opposition was harsh e.g. in 1919 the British army killed 400 peaceful protesters.

cards.title: Model answer: interwar nationalism in Africa and India
cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe nationalist movements in Africa and India between the two world wars.

steps.text: Africa – betrayal: Africans fought in WWI hoping for independence, but German colonies were given to Britain and France and colonial rule continued.
Africa – new leaders: young leaders educated abroad, such as Jomo Kenyatta, Leopold Senghor and Nnamdi Azikiwe, called for independence by the 1930s.
Ideas: Pan-Africanism (W.E.B. Du Bois, Marcus Garvey) to unite all black Africans, and Negritude, stressing the value of African culture.
India: Mahatma Gandhi led nonviolent protests and civil disobedience (satyagraha) against British rule.

cards.answer: Disappointed after WWI, a new educated generation in Africa (Kenyatta, Senghor, Azikiwe) used Pan-Africanism and Negritude, while Gandhi led nonviolent resistance in India.

cards.title: Completing this point: the road to the Second World War, step by step
body: **Root cause.** WWI and the harsh Treaty of Versailles, plus the aggressive fascist regimes in Germany, Italy and Japan.

**Germany.** Left the League (1933); announced an air force and raised the army from 100,000 to 500,000 (1935); reoccupied the Rhineland (1936); annexed Austria (1938); took the Sudetenland after Munich (1938), the rest of Czechoslovakia (1939); invaded **Poland on 1 September 1939** – Britain and France declared war two days later.
**Italy.** Invaded Ethiopia (1935); the League imposed sanctions.
**Japan.** Invaded **Manchuria in 1931**, left the League in 1933 and began full-scale war with China in **1937**.
**Appeasement and alliances.** Britain and France gave in to Hitler hoping for peace; the Rome–Berlin Axis and Anti-Comintern Pact (1936) and the Nazi–Soviet pact (1939) followed.
**Memory trick:** "Versailles, Villains, Victims, Vacillation (appeasement)."

cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the long-term causes of the Second World War.

steps.text: Aggression: Germany annexed Austria (1938) and invaded Czechoslovakia and Poland (1939); Italy invaded Ethiopia; Japan invaded China.
Versailles: Germany and Italy rejected the treaty – Hitler sent troops into the demilitarised Rhineland (1936) and rebuilt the army and air force (Luftwaffe).

cards.answer: Aggression by Germany, Italy and Japan, rejection of Versailles, Anglo-French appeasement and new alliances made war inevitable.

cards.title: The immediate cause of WW2
body: Hitler’s invasion of Poland on September 1, 1939.

cards.title: From Austria to Poland: the countdown to war, 1938–1939
body: **Step 1 – Austria (13 March 1938).** Hitler pressed Austria to admit German troops and annexed it; Britain and France did nothing serious.

**Step 2 – the Sudetenland (September 1938).** Germany demanded this German-speaking area of Czechoslovakia and threatened war. At the **Munich Conference** Britain and France agreed (appeasement) in return for Hitler's promise to make no more demands.
**Step 3 – the rest of Czechoslovakia (March 1939).** Hitler broke his promise; Britain and France now saw his ambition had no limit.
**Step 4 – Danzig and the guarantee.** When Hitler demanded the Polish port of Danzig, Britain and France promised to protect Poland.

**Step 5 – the Nazi–Soviet Pact (23 August 1939).** To avoid a two-front war, Hitler agreed with Stalin not to attack each other and secretly divided Eastern Europe: Finland, the Baltic states and eastern Poland to the USSR, western Poland to Germany.
**Step 6 – the invasion (1 September 1939).** Germany attacked Poland; two days later (3 September) Britain and France declared war.
**Memory trick:** "Austria, Sudeten, Prague, Pact, Poland" (A-S-P-P-P).
**Exam tip:** The invasion of Poland is the *immediate* cause; appeasement, Versailles and fascist expansion are the *long-term* causes.

cards.title: The course of the war
body: Even though Britain and France declared war on Germany on September 3, 1939, war did not begin automatically. Until April 1940, there was almost no war in Europe. That is why WWII was
Called a “phony war” at the beginning.
The war continued with fast military invasion of Denmark, Norway, Netherlands, Belgium & France one after another one by one in 1940.

The German forces attacked France troops by the Luxemburg and the Ardennes Forest (a forest found in Southeastern Belgium). 380,000 British forces who meant to help the French army trapped in DUNKRIK and successfully evacuated with the help of the British navy and Belgian civilians on April 1940.

With the help of Mussolini Hitler occupied France on June 22 1940 and replaced a Nazi leadership in France (known as Vichy France and was led by an aged French hero of the First World War named Marshal Petain.

The USA followed the policy of isolationism, though British asked for help US citizens don’t want their country to interfere. But US sent its military and logistic aid through its lend-lease act starting from 1941.
Hitler at first wasn’t sure to attack Britain or the USSR but decide to attack Britain first on august 1940 he launched air strike on Britain using the Luftwaffe.

The British retaliated in kind and bombed German cities, even though German air force attacked civilian cities British army couldn’t be easily defeated Hitler postponed British attack and decided to attack USSR by the operation of Barbosa.

Despite their initial success, a severe winter and strong Soviet resistance stopped the Germans. In December 1941, the Soviets carried out a successful counterattack, and thereby Germany’s plan collapsed.
On December 7, 1941, Japanese airplanes attacked US naval base at Pearl Harbor in the Hawaiian Islands which pulled the entry of USA to the war on the side of allies.
The United States declared war on Japan the next day. Three days later, Hitler declared war on the United States.

The entry of the United States into the war changed the balance of power between the Allied and Axis powers. Great Britain, the United States, and Soviet Union formed a coalition known as the Grand Alliance.

Until late 1942, Germany had the upper hand in the war. Its forces in North Africa, led by the famous general Erwin Rommel, were able to break through British defenses in Egypt and advanced toward Alexandria, but with us entry the war shifted to the favor of the allies.

cards.title: Completing this point: the fall of France and the Vichy regime
body: **The fall.** On 5 June 1940 Germany attacked southern France; five days later Mussolini declared war and invaded from the south. France surrendered on **22 June 1940**.
**Division.** Germany occupied about three-fifths of France; the rest was run by a German-controlled government at **Vichy** under Marshal **Pétain**, a WWI hero.

**Britain alone.** By 1940 Germany controlled western and central Europe except Britain, which asked the US for help; the US stayed officially isolationist but sent food, ships and weapons, and from **March 1941** Lend-Lease aid.
**Memory trick:** "June 22, 1940 – France falls; Vichy = Pétain."

cards.title: The defeat of Germany (European Theatre)
body: In North Africa, British forces stopped the advancing German troops at El Alamein in the summer of 1942.
In November 1942, British and American forces invaded French colonies in North Africa and forced German and Italian troops to surrender in May 1943.
The Germans were forced to surrender at Stalingrad and the entire sixth Germany army were encircled and completely smashed by the USSR troops on 2 February 1943.

Besides the war the Nazi Germany had done some atrocities towards other so called inferior races. By building concentration camps or simply shoot them down.one good example was the HOLOCAST were about six million Jews were exterminated in different camps. The largest and most infamous of the camps was Auschwitz.

Since 1943, the Allies had been planning to invade German occupied France from Britain across the English Channel. The Allies managed to trick the Germans into believing that the invasion would come on the flat plains of northern France. Instead, Allied forces under US General Dwight Eisenhower landed on the Normandy beaches on June 6, 1944. The invasion of Normandy, also known as D-Day invasion, is considered to be the largest naval invasion in history.

The Germans used newly developed tanks in their offensive. But, they were severely defeated by the Soviets at the Battle of Kursk, fought between 5 and 12 July 1943.The Battle of Kursk was the greatest tank battle of WWII.
Hitler committed suicide on April 30, two days after Mussolini was shot by Italian resistance fighters. On May 7, 1945, Germany surrendered and WWII was finally over in Europe.

cards.title: The war in Asia and the Pacific, step by step
body: **Pearl Harbor (7 December 1941).** Japan attacked the US base in Hawaii and, the same day, the Philippines and British Malaya; the USA declared war the next day and Hitler declared war on the USA three days later.

**Japanese expansion.** By spring 1942 Japan held almost all of Southeast Asia (including the Dutch East Indies) and much of the western Pacific. In the USA over 110,000 Japanese Americans were put in camps.
**The turn.** Allied forces stopped the Japanese advance and pushed them back island by island.

**The end.** Truman (president after Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945) feared huge losses in an invasion; atomic bombs fell on **Hiroshima (6 August)** and **Nagasaki (9 August)**, and Japan surrendered on **14 August 1945**.

cards.title: Consequences of the war
body: PoliticalConsequences: The war had many political consequences, among which were the following:
Germany, Italy and Japan were completely defeated and their totalitarian regimes were overthrown
The war weakened the economic, political and military power of Germany, Japan, Britain and France. In their place, the United States and the Soviet Union emerged as world superpowers.
The occupation of Eastern Europe by the USSR during the war led to the spread of communism in Europe.
The war led to the division of Germany into Soviet controlled East and US controlled West Germany

Rivalries among the wartime Allies emerged soon after the end of the war. These rivalries were characterized by economic, political, military and ideological struggles between the communist bloc led by the Soviet Union and the Western bloc led by the U.S.A.
The war resulted in the foundation of the United Nations Organization in 1945 to promote peace, security and international co-operation
The war also contributed to the process of decolonization in Africa and Asia by weakening the ability of European colonial powers to continue to hold onto their colonies.

cards.title: Completing this point: the economic and social consequences of WWII
body: **Economic.** Britain, France, Italy and Germany were bankrupted; industry, cities, transport and farms in Europe and Japan were destroyed, and 45 million homeless Europeans depended on US aid. Cost: over one trillion US dollars.

**Bombing of civilians.** London (from September 1940), German cities including **Dresden (1945)** where a firestorm killed about 100,000, Japanese cities from November 1944, and the atomic bombs on **Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945)**.
**Unemployment.** Millions of returning soldiers and prisoners needed jobs.
**Science and technology.** War research produced radar and other new devices.
**Memory trick:** "Broke, Bombed, Jobless – but Inventive."

cards.title: The economic consequences of WWII in detail
body: **Ruin in Europe and Japan.** Britain, France, Italy and Germany were bankrupted. Industrial regions everywhere except North America were destroyed; cities, roads, railways and communications were levelled, and farming was so damaged that Europe's **45 million homeless survivors** depended on US aid. The war cost more than **one trillion US dollars**.
**Unemployment.** Millions of returning soldiers and prisoners of war needed jobs.
**A new balance of power.** The USA came out of the war rich and strong, and the USSR became a military superpower, while Britain and France were too weak to keep their empires.

**Science pushed forward.** War research produced **radar**, the **jet engine**, mass production of **DDT** against malaria and **penicillin** for wounds – but also the atomic bomb, a terrifying example of technology used for destruction.
**Memory trick:** "Broke Europe, Rich America, Radar–Jet–DDT–Penicillin–Bomb."

cards.title: Social consequence
body: About 50 million army and civilian died and over 22 million became homeless.
Another important social consequence of WWII was the increased participation of women in economic and military sectors.

cards.title: The social consequences of WWII in detail
body: **Human loss.** Over **50 million** soldiers and civilians died, and over **21 million** people were left homeless.

**The Holocaust.** The Nazis believed in "Aryan" superiority and planned to exterminate the Jews. SS death squads shot almost one million; from 1942 Jews were sent by train to six death camps in occupied Poland, the largest being **Auschwitz**. About 30 % of arrivals were forced to work; the rest, especially the old, women and children, were gassed. In all **5–6 million Jews** were killed (about 90 % of the Jews of Poland, the Baltic states and Germany), as well as millions of Roma and Slavs.
**Forced migration.** After the war over **10 million Germans** were expelled from Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Romania into West Germany.
**Women.** Women fought in Soviet combat units and worked in industry and mines elsewhere, increasing their role in economic and military life.
**Memory trick:** "50 million dead, 21 million homeless, 6 million Jews, 10 million expelled."

cards.title: The end of Italian rule
body: With the huge army the Italians seems undefeated specially after they defeat the British arm and control Kassala, Galabat (in Sudan) and British Somali land in 1940.
Alarmed by the defeat the British soldiers led by general William Platt started counter attack and started pushing the Italians.

Before the British army started counter attack by using planes they started dropping pamphlets to the Eritrean people (Askaries were asked to give up arms or join the British army) promising them independence from the Eritrean people.
And the British army started to gain territories and in 1941 the Italians were defeated with the capture of Asmara in 1941.
The battle of Keren was one of the fiercest battles of WWII in East Africa which was fought for 12 days and ended in march 27 1941.

cards.title: The Battle of Keren (15–27 March 1941)
body: **Why the Italians lost.** Weakened by earlier defeats and with low morale, they lost thousands of Eritrean conscripts who defected, despite the strong terrain and reinforcements. After 12 days of the fiercest fighting in East Africa, **Keren fell on 27 March 1941**.
**Memory trick:** "Kassala → Agordat (1 Feb) → Barentu → Keren (27 March)."

cards.title: British Military Administration
body: Britain occupied Eritrea on behalf of the Allied powers. It declared Eritrea an “Occupied Enemy Territory.”

Britain was obliged to govern Eritrea according to the Hague Convention of 1907. The Convention obliged Britain to: Maintain peace and order in Eritrea Maintain the economic and social life of Eritreans Respect the organization and administration of the territory
For the first three years, the British army didn’t set up an army instead they preserved the Italians in offices and further gave them additional lands.

cards.title: New developments during the British period
body: The Eritrean economy began to deteriorate. Thousands of ex-askaris were left unemployed and inflation increased.
Asmara was overpopulated and suffered from acute shortages of food, housing and basic facilities.

Eritrea also suffered from security problems. Especially in the western lowlands, extensive conflicts emerged between the Beni Amir of Eritrea and Hadendewas of Sudan. The Tigres also started their struggle for emancipation from feudal domination.
Thus, the hope that the British would bring peace, prosperity and independence to Eritrea was eroded.

cards.title: TURNING POINT
body: On 3 August 1944 one article was posted on the Eritrean Weekly News (an official weekly newspaper sponsored by the BMA) under a pen name, Hade Eritrawi or One Eritrean. That wrote about the partition of Eritrea later the writer was known it was Brigadier Stephen H. Longrigg.

It created two opposing views within the members of Mahber Fqri Hager. Some members of the association supported the idea of union with Ethiopia and some expressed their desire for an independent Eritrea. The differing opinions about the future of Eritrea split Mahber Fqri Hager into two.

In reaction to the above mentioned problems and discontents. Some Eritrean legends such as shiek Ibrahim Sultan, fitewrari Gebremesqel Weldu ,Ras Tesema asmrom ,Weldab Weldwmariam Etc.formed the Mahber fqri hager party on May 5 1941.

The association elected an executive committee of twelve members with equal number of Muslims and Christians represented. From among them, Fiewrari Gebremeskel Woldu, Abdulkadir Kebire, and Fitewrari Haregot Abbay were elected president, vice president, and general secretary respectively.
The main objectives of Mahber Fiqri Hager were to present public grievances and serve as advisory body to the British Military Administration.
The differing opinions about the future of Eritrea split Mahber Fqri Hager into two.
The Ethiopian government started to infiltrate the association using Orthodox clerk’s such one was the famous Abune Marqos who changed the association name to MAHBER FQRI HAGER ERITRA MS ETHIOPIA.
In reaction to this some prominent leaders like WEL-WEL, SHIEK IBRAHIM SULTAN, DEGIAT ALI HASSEN, AND DEGIAT ABREHA TESEMA formed the ERITREA N ERITRAWYAN party separated from Mahber fqri hager.
Even though BMA did not allow open political activities; both Eritrea for Eritreans and Association of Love for Country Eritrea with Ethiopia began to campaign for support among the Eritrean society.
